questions.question: Why does log₂8 = 3, and what single question does every logarithm ask?
questions.solution: Because 2³ = 8. Every logarithm asks: 'to what POWER must the base be raised to give this number?' The log is the exponent — log_b(x) = y ⇔ b^y = x. Keeping that equivalence in mind converts log problems into exponent problems.

questions.concept: Log laws come from exponent laws
questions.question: Derive log(mn) = log m + log n from the definition of logarithm.
questions.solution: Let m = b^x, n = b^y. Then mn = b^x·b^y = b^(x+y) — exponent laws turn MULTIPLICATION into ADDITION of exponents. Reading the last equation as a logarithm: log(mn) = x + y = log m + log n. Every log rule is an exponent rule in disguise.

questions.concept: Quadratic — nature of roots via discriminant
questions.question: For ax² + bx + c = 0, explain what the discriminant b² − 4ac tells you, and why the square root of a negative discriminant signals no real root.
questions.solution: The quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac))/2a — the discriminant sits under the square root. D > 0: two distinct real roots; D = 0: one repeated root; D < 0: √ of a negative number — no real value, so no real roots (two complex ones). The discriminant measures how far the parabola's vertex sits from the x-axis.

questions.question: Why does a quadratic with roots α, β equal x² − (α+β)x + αβ? Use factorisation.
questions.solution: If α and β are roots, the polynomial factors as (x−α)(x−β) = x² − (α+β)x + αβ. Matching with ax² + bx + c: sum = −b/a, product = c/a. Constructing a quadratic from its roots (or reading the roots from coefficients) is direct coefficient matching.

questions.question: Distinguish a sequence from a series, and state what Σ notation adds.
questions.solution: A sequence is an ordered LIST of terms (a₁, a₂, a₃, …); a series is the SUM of those terms. Σ compresses 'add these terms following this rule' — e.g. Σn² from 1 to 5 = 1+4+9+16+25. The distinction matters because sequences have patterns of TERMS while series ask about SUMS (which may converge).

questions.concept: Why a quadratic can have no real roots
questions.question: x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution, yet the quadratic formula still returns values. What is the discriminant telling you?
questions.solution: The discriminant b² − 4ac is negative, so the square root is not real; the parabola y = x² + 1 lies entirely above the x-axis and never crosses it. The formula still yields the correct COMPLEX roots. A negative discriminant signals 'no real intersection', not 'no answer' — the solutions exist, just outside the reals.

questions.concept: Why the sum of roots is −b/a
questions.question: For ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots α and β, why is α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a?
questions.solution: Factorise identically: ax² + bx + c = a(x − α)(x − β) = a[x² − (α+β)x + αβ]. Matching coefficients gives b = −a(α+β) and c = aαβ, so α+β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. The relations come from comparing two expressions for the same polynomial — an identity, not a coincidence.

questions.concept: Why arithmetic and geometric means differ
questions.question: For any two positive numbers the geometric mean never exceeds the arithmetic mean. Why, and when are they equal?
questions.solution: AM − GM = (a+b)/2 − √(ab) = (√a − √b)²/2 ≥ 0. The square is never negative, and it is zero exactly when a = b. GM is the side of a square with the same area as an a × b rectangle; AM is half the perimeter. They coincide only for a square — equality is the symmetric case.
